title: Next Greater Element II
description:
Given a circular integer array `nums` (meaning the element immediately after `nums[nums.length - 1]` is `nums[0]`), return an array `result` of the same length where `result[i]` is the **next greater number** for `nums[i]`.

The next greater number of `nums[i]` is the first element strictly greater than `nums[i]` encountered when traversing forward from index `i` in circular order (wrapping around from the end of the array back to index `0`). If no such strictly greater element exists in the entire array, set `result[i]` to `-1`.
hints: Simulate the circular array by conceptually iterating through the array twice (`0` to `2n - 1`) using modulo indexing `i % n`.
Maintain a monotonic decreasing stack of indices whose next greater element has not yet been found.
When the current element `nums[i % n]` is strictly greater than `nums[stack[-1]]`, pop from the stack and record `nums[i % n]` as its answer. Only push indices during the first pass (`i < n`).

examples.explanation: For nums[0] = 1, the next greater element is 2. For nums[1] = 2, no greater element exists (-1). For nums[2] = 1, wrapping around yields 2.
Each element finds the next strictly larger value clockwise; 4 is the maximum so its answer is -1, while the trailing 3 wraps around to 4.
5 has no greater element (-1). Every other element wraps around the circular array to reach 5.

title: Daily Temperatures
description:
Given an array of integers `temperatures` representing the daily temperatures, return an array `answer` of the same length such that `answer[i]` is the number of days you must wait after the `i`-th day to observe a strictly warmer temperature.

If there is no future day with a strictly warmer temperature than `temperatures[i]`, set `answer[i]` to `0`.
hints: For each day, you need the index of the first subsequent day with a strictly higher temperature.
Keep a monotonic decreasing stack of day indices whose warmer day has not yet been seen.
Whenever today's temperature exceeds the temperature at the top index of the stack, pop that index `prev` and set `answer[prev] = i - prev`.

examples.explanation: Day 0 (73) waits 1 day for 74; day 2 (75) waits 4 days for 76; days 6 (76) and 7 (73) have no warmer future day.
Temperatures increase every day, so every day except the last waits exactly 1 day.
Each day is immediately followed by a warmer day except the final day.

title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
description:
Given an array of non-negative integers `heights` representing the heights of bars in a histogram where the width of each bar is `1`, return the area of the largest axis-aligned rectangle that can be formed completely inside the histogram.

A rectangle spanning contiguous bars `[l, r]` has width `r - l + 1` and maximum possible height `min(heights[l], heights[l + 1], ..., heights[r])`.
hints: Any maximal rectangle is bounded in height by at least one bar `i`. Its maximum width extends left to the nearest shorter bar and right to the nearest shorter bar.
Maintain a monotonic increasing stack of bar indices. When a shorter bar arrives at index `i`, every taller bar popped from the stack has `i` as its right boundary.
After popping index `idx`, the new stack top (or `-1` if empty) is its left boundary, giving width `i - left - 1`. Append a sentinel `0` height at the end to flush remaining bars.

examples.explanation: Bars at indices 2 and 3 (heights 5 and 6) form a rectangle of height 5 and width 2, giving area 10.
A rectangle of height 2 spanning both bars has area 2 * 2 = 4, equal to the single bar of height 4.
The single bar of height 9 forms a rectangle of area 9.

title: Maximal Rectangle
description:
Given a `rows x cols` binary matrix filled with characters `'0'` and `'1'`, find the largest axis-aligned sub-rectangle containing only `'1'`s and return its area.

If the matrix contains no `'1'`s, return `0`.
hints: Consider fixing the bottom edge of the rectangle at each row `r`. Each column then has a height equal to the number of consecutive `'1'`s ending at row `r`.
This reduces each row to an instance of Largest Rectangle in Histogram over the column heights array.
Update `heights[c] = heights[c] + 1` if `matrix[r][c] == '1'` else `0`, and compute the max histogram area in `O(cols)` using a monotonic increasing stack.

examples.explanation: The maximal rectangle of '1's spans rows 1..2 and columns 2..4, which is a 2x3 rectangle of area 6.
There are no '1's in the matrix, so the maximal area is 0.
The single cell '1' forms a 1x1 rectangle of area 1.

title: Online Stock Span
description:
Design an algorithm that collects daily price quotes for a stock and returns the **span** of that stock's price for the current day.

The **span** of the stock's price on the current day is defined as the maximum number of consecutive days (starting from today and going backward) for which the stock price was **less than or equal to** today's price.

Implement the `StockSpanner` class:
- `StockSpanner()` initializes the object of the class.
- `int next(int price)` returns the span of the stock's price given that today's price is `price`.
constraints: At most 10^4 calls will be made to next.
hints: If today's price is greater than or equal to yesterday's price, today's span absorbs yesterday's entire span.
Maintain a monotonic strictly decreasing stack of `(price, span)` pairs.
For each `next(price)`, initialize `span = 1`, pop all pairs with `top.price <= price` while adding their spans to `span`, then push `(price, span)` and return `span`.

examples.explanation: Prices [100,80,60,70,60,75,85] produce spans [1,1,1,2,1,4,6]. For 75, the 4 consecutive days [60,70,60,75] are all <= 75.
Each strictly increasing price absorbs all previous days, yielding spans 1, 2, 3, 4.

title: Sliding Window Maximum
description:
You are given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k` representing the size of a sliding window that moves from the very left of the array to the very right, one position at a time.

At each position, you can only see the `k` elements currently inside the window. Return an array of length `nums.length - k + 1` containing the maximum element in each sliding window from left to right.
hints: Any element inside the window that is smaller than or equal to a newer element to its right can never become the window maximum again.
Maintain a deque of indices whose corresponding values in `nums` are strictly decreasing from front to back.

Before pushing index `i`, remove indices from the back with values `<= nums[i]`, and remove the front index if it has fallen out of the window (`dq[0] <= i - k`). The front index always holds the current window's maximum.

examples.explanation: A single-element array with window size 1 has only one window [1] with maximum 1.
The single window covers the entire array [9, 11], whose maximum is 11.

title: Constrained Subsequence Sum
description:
Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the maximum sum of a **non-empty** subsequence of `nums` such that for every two consecutive elements `nums[i]` and `nums[j]` in the subsequence (with `i < j`), the index gap satisfies `j - i <= k`.

A subsequence of an array is obtained by deleting zero or more elements from the array while preserving the relative order of the remaining elements.
hints: Let `dp[i]` be the maximum constrained subsequence sum ending at index `i`. Then `dp[i] = nums[i] + max(0, max_{i-k <= j < i} dp[j])`.
Computing `max_{i-k <= j < i} dp[j]` directly takes `O(k)` per index, which is too slow when `k` is large.
Use a monotonic decreasing deque of indices `(j, dp[j])` over the sliding window `[i - k, i - 1]` to retrieve the maximum previous `dp` value in `O(1)` amortized time.

examples.explanation: Pick subsequence [10, 2, 5, 20] (indices 0, 1, 3, 4; all consecutive gaps <= 2), yielding 10 + 2 + 5 + 20 = 37.
The subsequence must be non-empty, so choosing the single largest element [-1] gives -1.

title: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K
description:
Given an integer array `nums` (which may contain negative numbers, zeros, and positive numbers) and a positive integer `k`, return the length of the shortest **non-empty contiguous subarray** of `nums` whose sum is at least `k`.

If no contiguous subarray has a sum greater than or equal to `k`, return `-1`.
hints: Because `nums` can contain negative numbers, a standard two-pointer sliding window fails. Rewrite subarray sums using prefix sums `P[j] - P[i] >= k` with `i < j`.

Maintain a monotonic increasing deque of prefix sum indices. If `P[i] >= P[j]` for `i < j`, then `i` is strictly worse than `j` for all future endpoints (larger prefix sum and farther left), so pop `i` from the back.

Whenever `P[j] - P[dq[0]] >= k`, update the answer with `j - dq[0]` and pop `dq[0]` from the front because any future `j' > j` would only form a longer subarray with `dq[0]`. Use 64-bit integers (`long`) for prefix sums.

examples.explanation: The single-element subarray [1] has sum 1 >= 1 and length 1.
Even the full array [1, 2] sums to 3 < 4, so return -1.
Only the full array [2, -1, 2] reaches sum 3 >= 3, giving length 3.

title: Sum of Subarray Minimums
description:
Given an array of integers `arr`, find the sum of `min(b)` over every non-empty contiguous subarray `b` of `arr`.

Since the total sum can be very large, return the answer modulo `10^9 + 7`.
hints: Instead of enumerating every subarray, count how many subarrays have `arr[i]` as their minimum and add `arr[i] * count`.

To avoid double-counting when duplicate values exist, break ties consistently: find the nearest strictly smaller element to the left (`<`) and the nearest smaller-or-equal element to the right (`<=`).

A single pass with a monotonic increasing stack computes both boundaries simultaneously: when index `mid` is popped by a smaller-or-equal element at `i`, `mid` spans `(mid - left) * (i - mid)` subarrays.

examples.explanation: Summing the minimum across all 15 contiguous subarrays gives 444.
All 6 contiguous subarrays have minimum 1, so the sum is 6.

solutionCode.python:
class Solution:
    def sumSubarrayMins(self, arr: List[int]) -> int:
        MOD = 10**9 + 7
        n = len(arr)
        stack = []
        total = 0
        for i in range(n + 1):
            cur = arr[i] if i < n else 0
            while stack and arr[stack[-1]] >= cur:
                mid = stack.pop()
                left = stack[-1] if stack else -1
                total = (total + arr[mid] * (mid - left) * (i - mid)) % MOD
            stack.append(i)
        return total

title: Number of Visible People in a Queue
description:
There are `n` people standing in a queue, numbered from `0` to `n - 1` from left to right. You are given an integer array `heights` of **distinct** positive integers where `heights[i]` represents the height of the `i`-th person.

Person `i` can **see** another person `j` to their right (`i < j`) if and only if everyone standing between them is shorter than both of them. Formally, person `i` can see person `j` when `i < j` and `min(heights[i], heights[j]) > max(heights[i + 1], heights[i + 2], ..., heights[j - 1])` (vacuously true when `j == i + 1`).

Return an array `answer` of length `n` where `answer[i]` is the number of people person `i` can see to their right in the queue.
constraints: All values of heights are unique.
hints: Process the queue from right to left while maintaining a monotonic decreasing stack of heights currently visible from the left.
For person `i`, pop every person from the stack shorter than `heights[i]`: person `i` can see each of them, and nobody to the left of `i` will be able to see past `i` to those shorter people.
After popping shorter people, if the stack is still non-empty, person `i` can also see the first taller person on top of the stack (add `1` to the count), then push `heights[i]`.

examples.explanation: Person 0 (10) sees 6, 8, and 11 (count 3). Person 1 (6) sees 8. Person 2 (8) sees 5 and 11. Person 5 (9) sees no one to their right.
Person 0 (5) sees all four people to their right (1, 2, 3, 10) because each is taller than everyone before them in the gap.
Every person except the last immediately hits a taller neighbor and sees exactly 1 person.

title: 132 Pattern
description:
Given an array of `n` integers `nums`, a **132 pattern** is a subsequence of three elements `nums[i]`, `nums[j]`, and `nums[k]` such that `i < j < k` and `nums[i] < nums[k] < nums[j]`.

Return `true` if there exists at least one 132 pattern in `nums`, and `false` otherwise.
hints: Think about fixing the middle element `nums[j]` (the '3') or scanning from right to left to find the best possible '2' (`nums[k]`) paired with some '3' to its left.

Traverse from right to left with a monotonic decreasing stack of candidate '3' values, and maintain `third`: the largest value popped from the stack so far (guaranteed to have a strictly larger '3' to its left).
If you encounter `nums[i] < third`, then `(nums[i], corresponding '3', third)` forms a valid 132 pattern. Otherwise pop all stack elements `< nums[i]` to update `third`, then push `nums[i]`.

examples.explanation: The array is strictly increasing, so no triplet satisfies nums[i] < nums[k] < nums[j].
The subsequence [1, 4, 2] at indices (1, 2, 3) satisfies 1 < 2 < 4.
Several 132 patterns exist, such as [-1, 3, 2], [-1, 3, 0], and [-1, 2, 0].
